claims.text: Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo is a disordered BCC refractory high-entropy alloy.
Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo has a room-temperature compressive yield strength of approximately 1719 MPa.
The high Mo content increases the alloy's electronegativity difference and is associated with reduced plasticity.
A moderate fraction of Mo should be replaced by V to form NbZrTiHfMo1-xVx alloys.
Replacing Mo with V will improve the room-temperature compressive strength-plasticity balance.
Replacing Mo with V reduces the overall electronegativity difference of NbZrTiHfMo.
V substitution produces larger atomic-volume misfits and greater local lattice or atomic-spacing fluctuations.
Lattice distortion and modulus mismatch are important sources of solid-solution strengthening in single-phase multi-principal BCC alloys.
Reducing electronegativity mismatch lowers abrupt local stress fields.
The V-induced volume misfits and lattice fluctuations facilitate dislocation movement and improve plasticity.
V-induced volume misfits continue to provide solid-solution strengthening.
Local solute-concentration fluctuations can pin dislocations and create high barriers to dislocation motion in random alloys.
The V-modified alloy will have a higher room-temperature compressive plastic strain before failure than the equiatomic baseline.
The V-modified alloy will retain similar compressive yield strength or suffer only a slight reduction relative to 1719 MPa.
The beneficial effect requires retention of a homogeneous, disordered BCC structure during room-temperature compression.
The improvement should occur only within an approximately 10-25 at.% V substitution range.
Beyond the proposed substitution range, BCC phase stability may be compromised or strengthening may deteriorate.

contradictions.description: The text calls x = 0.10-0.25 a 10-25 total-at.% V substitution, but the formula NbZrTiHfMo1-xVx keeps the Mo-plus-V sublattice at one of five equal formula units. After normalization, x = 0.10-0.25 corresponds to only 2-5 total at.% V. The intended compositions are therefore internally inconsistent or ambiguous.

The hypothesis says larger V-induced volume misfits and lattice fluctuations facilitate dislocation motion, while also invoking fluctuation-induced dislocation pinning and solid-solution strengthening. A dual effect is possible, but no criterion explains when the same fluctuations reduce rather than increase the barrier to glide.
